question: What is the meaning of return options in relation to customer  information?
description: Return options in relation to customer information refer to the process of determining who owns the relevant data or passport when a structure, construction element, or product is no longer in use and is ready to be reused. It involves understanding the ownership of the data during the period when the structure is not actively in use and deciding how the information will be managed and transferred if materials are removed or if ownership of the structure changes hands.

6.9.3 Ownership  
An owner is an organisation, and that organisation has to commit itself 
to the guideline of publicly announcing whether it will manage the data 
itself or arrange this through third parties. 
Every passport is part of a decomposition structure of a higher level. 
The owner of an area or structure also owns the underlying parts. 
This is different for lease or other service agreements. As part of the 
circular economy, service contracts which show other owners in a 
decomposition have become much more common. Arrangements can 
be made for each project about how ownership will change if materials 
are removed. 
As regards ownership, it is important to know when the structure, 
construction element or product will come back onto the market to 
be reused (15, 50, 75 or even up to 200 years). Who owns the 
relevant data or passport in the meantime, and what information do 
they contain? 
Traditionally, a structure including all construction elements is handed 
over to the owner, even if a building is sold on to another owner after 
its completion. This means that the owner also owns all the 
components. A completion document is provided for this. This 
information is necessary in the event of maintenance to ensure it is 
properly carried out. 
The construction elements and products present will have to be 
mapped at the end of the structure's life. The issue then is an element's 
or product's residual value. This will quite probably be different 
information from that needed for delivery or maintenance. However, it 
is still connected to the object. When elements or products are sold, 
they will be accompanied by the necessary information. 
Of course, a future situation may arise where the owner of a structure 
is only the user of the structure and the supplier remains responsible 
for maintenance and ownership. This is great from a cradle-to-cradle 
philosophy. A supplier then takes back its own products. It has all the 
data. If a supplier is taken over or otherwise acquired, this information 
will still be of value to the person who subsequently takes on the 
product. 
In all cases, the warranty period and the accompanying liability must be 
clearly defined. Since it would be difficult to keep a supplier eternally 
responsible for managing the product specifications, we recommend 
transferring this responsibility to the owner of the object. A company's 
‘trade secrets’ will have to be taken into account however. No 
conclusive answer is available yet to the question of where this 
information goes if a business is discontinued or changes ownership. 
Ownership is addressed in more detail in 7.2.2 ‘Ownership and 
management of data’.  
6.9.4 Privacy  
Once the need for a circular economy had been established, the issue 
of ensuring sufficient legal protection against breaches of people's 
rights to privacy also emerged. 
In order to arrive at a system of circular information exchange, the 
information will have to be separated from personal information. And 
the guidelines for data owners will have to become more stringent. 
At present, a Privacy Impact Assessment is being carried out to 
demonstrate the residual risks after separation. 
6.10  Transparency 
Asset managers should make their data publicly available so that 
interested parties can gain access to the composition of available

• Difficulties to extract material from used products at an equal high 
quality of raw material extraction (Malmgren and M¨otsch Larsson, 
2020). 
Component manufacturer  
• Access to new markets because of quality information of material and 
object components (Hansen et al., 2018; Munaro and Tavares, 2021; 
Smeets et al., 2019).  
• Proposition value of CE-based products (or proper mix between new 
and CE-based products) (Debacker and Manshoven, 2016; Munaro 
and Tavares, 2021).  
• Potential cost reduction (lower testing, reconditioning and fabrication 
costs enabled by technical/usage data) through re-use or remanu­
facturing (Smeets et al., 2019).  
• Uncertain quality of resources (Malmgren and M¨otsch Larsson, 2020; 
Wittenveen & Bos, 2018).  
• Inaccurate spare part or material availability prediction (Malmgren 
and M¨otsch Larsson, 2020; Spengler and Schr¨oter, 2003; Wittenveen 
& Bos, 2018).  
• Lack of standardized components and materials which facilitates 
inter-operable reuse (Honic et al., 2019a).  
• Potential liability issues when materials are reused (Debacker and 
Manshoven, 2016).  
• Data provision costs (Rudolphi, 2018).  
• Firms lack of willingness to be transparent (Rudolphi, 2018).  
• Confidentiality issues (Rudolphi, 2018).  
• Attitude transition from sell faster and more, towards get paid to 
deliver the most circular product (Malmgren and M¨otsch Larsson, 
2020).  
• Adapting to reverse logistics requires searching new CE sourcing 
partners (Malmgren and M¨otsch Larsson, 2020).

• Feedback  
• Life cycle feedback of objects (e.g. material choices) to make better

• Understanding the preference/use of an object by the end-user to 
optimize the product design for user experience (Debacker and 
Manshoven, 2016).  
• Better value proposition

• Standardization improves circularity but limits design freedom for

Contractor (incl. assembler)  
• Better proposition  
• Information availability (e.g., IoT-based maintenance prediction) 
extends life-time of an object and reduces maintenance costs, which 
may be a propositional advantage in long-term licensed-based ser­
vice contracting (Bouwend Nederland, 2020; Chahine, 2021; 
Debacker and Manshoven, 2016; Munaro and Tavares, 2021).  
• To improve the residual value and current (CE) performance of 
their buildings (Bouwend Nederland, 2020; Hansen et al., 2018).  
• Data provision costs (do not yet out wage the benefits but are 
expected to do so in the near future as data management cost will 
decrease because (1) it becomes a general practice and (2) 
environmental cost are expected to rise) (Bouwend Nederland, 
2020).  
• Smaller firms typically lack behind in information management and 
will have incurred costs with adopting a passport (Bouwend 
Nederland, 2020).
